about: Pure Earth Organisation Uganda is a Ugandan environmental and sustainable development organisation established in 2022, committed to advancing environmental conservation, sustainable waste management and community-led climate action.

We believe that environmental challenges require practical, inclusive and innovative solutions. Our work focuses on transforming waste into valuable resources, promoting responsible environmental practices and empowering communities to help build a cleaner, healthier and more sustainable environment.

Through community engagement, environmental education, plastic waste recycling, skills development and strategic partnerships, we work with young people, women, schools, local communities and marginalised groups to create opportunities for environmental sustainability and improved livelihoods.
At Pure Earth, we see waste not simply as an environmental problem, but also as an opportunity for innovation, entrepreneurship and sustainable development.
vision: A cleaner, greener and more sustainable planet where communities live in harmony with the environment.
mission: To promote sustainable waste management, environmental conservation and inclusive community development through innovation, education, partnerships and practical environmental solutions.

areas.title: Sustainable waste management and plastic recycling
areas.text: We promote responsible waste management, plastic collection, recycling and waste-to-value initiatives that reduce pollution while creating opportunities for resource recovery and green entrepreneurship.

areas.title: Climate action and environmental conservation
areas.text: We support community-led climate action through environmental awareness, conservation initiatives, climate education and practical interventions that build environmental resilience.

areas.title: Environmental education and community engagement
areas.text: We engage schools, young people and local communities through environmental education, school environmental clubs, awareness campaigns and community clean-ups.

areas.title: Youth and women's empowerment
areas.text: We equip young people and women with knowledge, practical skills and opportunities to take part in the green economy, environmental entrepreneurship and sustainable livelihoods.

areas.title: Inclusive environmental development
areas.text: We promote the participation of persons with disabilities and other underserved groups, because sustainable development must be inclusive and accessible to everyone.

principles.title: Innovation
principles.text: Developing practical and locally relevant solutions to environmental challenges.

principles.title: Community participation
principles.text: Placing communities at the centre of environmental decision-making and action.

principles.title: Sustainability
principles.text: Promoting solutions that deliver lasting environmental and social benefits.

principles.title: Inclusion

principles.text: Working with schools, civil society organisations, local governments, development partners and other stakeholders on shared environmental goals.

impact: Through our programmes, we have engaged and trained over 100 young people in environmental action and sustainable practices. We also work with schools to strengthen environmental awareness, establish environmental clubs, promote responsible waste disposal and encourage practical conservation activities.
future: We envision communities where waste is valued as a resource, young people are active participants in the green economy, women have opportunities to lead environmental initiatives, and everyone has a role in protecting the planet.

projects.title: A dustbin made from the waste it collects
projects.lede: The Pure Earth Innovation Hub turns used plastic bottles into dustbins, then puts them where children will use them every day.
body: Every bin is a lesson you can walk past. It is built from used plastic bottles, so pupils can see exactly what a discarded bottle can become.

In April 2026, in partnership with TARD Foundation and Gufasha Girls Foundation, we took the bins to Kayunga Mixed Primary School. Each one carries a simple notice: Dump. Keep our environment clean. Use it. Respect it. This dustbin is made from plastic bottles.
Pupils, teachers and our team gathered behind signs that carried the message further: There is no Plan B. I am a climate educator. Clean air = stronger lungs. Green school = a happy planet.

projects.title: From bottles to bins and planters
projects.lede: What others throw away becomes something people want to keep. That is the idea behind our waste-to-value work.
body: Our earliest bins were made from green and clear bottles fixed around metal rings, using material that was already lying around.
Women now build taller bins around wooden frames, adding row after row of bottle mesh until the frame is covered. It is practical work that people can learn together.
By June 2024 the same bottles were also becoming planters and decorative pieces, displayed alongside painted tyre planters. Each piece shows that plastic waste can be turned into something of value.

projects.title: Lessons under the tent, trees in the ground
projects.lede: We start with a conversation about climate, then hand pupils a seedling so they can act on it the same day.
body: The day began under a large tent. Pupils filled the benches while facilitators worked through climate and environment topics at the blackboard and took questions from raised hands.
Then everyone went outside. Seedlings arrived in the boot of a car, and small groups of pupils dug, planted and watered trees around the compound with facilitators kneeling beside them.
Planting in small groups means every child touches the soil, and every class has a tree to look after once the visitors have gone.

projects.title: Today, recycle for a better tomorrow
projects.place: Murchison Bay Primary School and the community
projects.lede: Some of our most direct campaigning is done with marker pens, paper and a walk through the neighbourhood.
body: In November 2023 young people carried handwritten messages along community roads: Recycle more plastic wastes. Use it up, wear it out, make it do or do without. Today, recycle for a better tomorrow.

The same day we were with pupils at Murchison Bay Primary School, close to our home in Luzira. Earlier that month another young campaigner summed up the whole approach on a single sheet of paper: Refuse, reduce, re-use, repurpose, recycle plastics.

projects.title: Taking climate adaptation to the village
projects.lede: While world leaders met at the UN General Assembly, we joined partners in a rural community to talk about what climate change means at home.
body: Women, men and children sat together under the trees for a community meeting, while our team and partners moved through the village with a megaphone and placards.
The messages were direct: The one way of tackling climate impacts in Africa is through adaptation. There is no climate justice without loss and damage finance.
Tree planting tied the day together under a line shared from the visit: Plant a tree, save the generation.

projects.title: Carrying the message to decision makers
projects.place: Masulita Parish and the 3rd CEO's Breakfast Meeting
projects.lede: Change also needs people in the room. In 2026 the message reached a high-level stage and a parish commemoration.
body: At the 3rd CEO's Breakfast Meeting and High-Level Dialogue on Green Economy, Sustainability and SDGs, schoolgirls walked on stage with brooms, a seedling and a bottle dustbin, putting a practical waste solution in front of business and policy leaders.
On 7 June 2026 we joined the World Environment Day commemoration at Masulita Parish, standing with communities and other organisations for environmental justice.
